title: USCIS Enhanced Background Checks Delay Green Cards, Naturalization Cases Nationwide
excerpt: A sweeping new fingerprint-based vetting process tied to expanded FBI database access has effectively paused approvals across major immigration case types since April.
body:
• USCIS began enhanced fingerprint-based background checks on April 27, 2026, effectively pausing approvals across green card, naturalization, asylum and employment-based applications.
  • The changes stem from Executive Order 14385, which expanded USCIS access to FBI criminal history databases through the Next Generation Identification system.
  • Officers must resubmit fingerprints for all pending cases where biometrics were collected before April 27, creating a processing bottleneck.
  • Physicians were exempted from the holds in May 2026, but most other applicants remain subject to delays with no public timeline for resolution.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has implemented a sweeping new security vetting process that has delayed approvals across a wide range of immigration case types, affecting hundreds of thousands of applicants with pending green card, naturalization and employment-based petitions.

The enhanced background checks took effect on April 27, 2026, after USCIS gained expanded access to FBI criminal history databases, according to internal agency guidance first reported by CBS News and confirmed by Reuters. The changes stem from Executive Order 14385, signed by President Trump on February 6, 2026, which directed federal criminal justice agencies to share criminal history record information with the Department of Homeland Security to the fullest extent permitted by law.

How the New System Works

Under the updated protocol, USCIS must resubmit fingerprint information for most pending applications in which biometrics were collected before April 27, according to an analysis by law firm Clark Hill. In most cases, the agency will use fingerprints already on file rather than requiring applicants to attend new Application Support Center appointments.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=HPsc5v5kgqA

Already-scheduled interviews are expected to proceed, but the issuance of final approvals has been largely paused until the new checks are completed. Officers have also reportedly been instructed not to initiate new fingerprint checks for cases they intend to deny, meaning the additional screening is focused primarily on cases moving toward approval.

"USCIS has implemented new security checks to strengthen the vetting and screening of applicants through expanded access to federal criminal databases."

— USCIS spokesman, in a statement to U.S. media

The affected case types include adjustment of status applications, naturalization petitions, asylum claims, family-based petitions, humanitarian applications and employment-based filings, according to legal analyses by Clark Hill and Duane Morris.

Broader Vetting Overhaul

The fingerprint reprocessing is part of a broader vetting overhaul that USCIS outlined in a March 30 public alert. The agency said it had found that prior screening measures were "wholly inadequate" and that some individuals had been naturalized or granted permanent residence who should not have been.

Additional measures include shortened validity periods for certain employment authorization documents, expanded social media and financial vetting, biometric identity verification updates and the launch of Operation PARRIS — a program of additional background checks, re-interviews and merit reviews of refugee claims conducted by the USCIS Vetting Center.

The agency also began weighing country-specific risk factors in adjudications following a November 2025 policy alert tied to Presidential Proclamation 10949, which restricted entry from 39 countries deemed to lack adequate vetting infrastructure.

Physician Exemption

In early May 2026, USCIS quietly lifted adjudication holds for cases involving foreign physicians, allowing their applications to resume processing, Clark Hill reported. The exemption applies to immigration benefits associated with physicians, including H-1B petitions, J-1 waiver applications and employment-based immigrant petitions.

The carve-out reflected growing concern about the impact of processing delays on the U.S. healthcare system. Foreign-trained physicians make up a significant portion of the medical workforce, and the pause had raised alarms about staffing shortages and disruptions to patient care. The agency did not issue a formal announcement of the change.

What Applicants Should Expect

USCIS said in a statement to U.S. media that "any delay in decision issuance should be brief and resolved shortly." Immigration attorneys, however, have described the impact as more significant. With expanded access to detailed criminal history data, USCIS may issue more Requests for Evidence and Notices of Intent to Deny, including for matters that previously drew less scrutiny such as non-conviction arrests, juvenile records or sealed cases, according to Clark Hill.

The agency has begun lifting holds for certain categories beyond physicians, including petitions filed by U.S. citizens, intercountry adoption forms, certain special immigrant visa petitions and asylum applications from countries not designated as high-risk. But many applicants remain subject to holds pending completion of the new fingerprint-based checks.

Immigration attorneys have advised applicants to monitor their case status for movement and to prepare for potentially extended processing times as USCIS works through the backlog created by the re-vetting requirement.
